items.title: The Ladybird Browser Reaches Alpha
items.summary: If we learned one thing form the browser wars of the 2000s, it’s that having a single ecosystem dominate the internet is best avoided. Yet here we are in 2026, and through Google’s Blink and Apple’s Webkit, we have very little diversity in the world of web browsing engines. Firefox is now very much an outsider, and that’s pretty much it. But there is another up-and-coming fully-featured browser, Ladybird, and it’s now available in alpha form for those of you with macOS or Linux. This browser had an unlikely start, as a component of the esoteric operating system, SerenityOS. We tested it in that form and found it competent, but the process of running the OS in a VM, not so much. It was split into a separate project in 2024, and since then they have been working towards this point, of having something close to a release version. We’ve followed Ladybird for a while now, not because we expect the world to adopt it en masse, but because, incredibly, it’s now the third major in-development browser engine family. Just as we needed the Konqueror-derived Webkit a couple of decades ago to provide a balance to the then-dominant Internet Explorer, we may need this piece of software at some point. We’ll give it a try, and perhaps you will too. This makes me think that a good next target for an AI assisted software liberation would probably be web browsers. Yes, Firefox is open source, but the official releases are all run by a group of opinionated people who do it for a living. That financial support requirement understandably makes people conservative about taking risks. A modern AI assisted fork of any open source browser could do great things. items.title: Watch This (Virtual) Mechanical Watch Do Its Thing
items.summary: Normally, when we write about watches, they are the electronic kind. But we’re also fascinated by mechanical watches. It is amazing that these mechanisms have existed for centuries. [Martin C. Martin] is fascinated too, and he produced a page that explains how they work simply and also includes wonderful 3D animations that make it all clear. If you are just skimming the page, be sure to drag the animations to spin them around. He was inspired by another page that has even more detailed information and different animations. It turns out the hairspring was invented by [Christiaan Huygens], who is also known for many other scientific advances in optics, astronomy, mathematics, and more. The main idea is that if you fix the far end of the spring and let the center rotate, the spring will wind and unwind at a constant rate. Combined with a balance wheel to slow the hairspring, you have a wheel that oscillates back and forth at a fairly constant rate. According to the post, a well-calibrated mechanical watch should lose about nine seconds a day. Given that there are 86,400 seconds in a day, that’s not bad (just a hair over 0.01%). Of course, without some other mechanism, you’d have a metronome swinging back and forth as the spring moved. That’s why there’s also an escapement that converts the back-and-forth motion into a toothed escape wheel. It wants to spin as a consequence of the unwinding of the mainspring (another spiral spring). This is the one you are cranking when you wind the watch. However, the escapement tied to the hairspring prevents the escape wheel from moving more than one step for each tick of the hairspring. The mainspring tries to turn the escape wheel. items.title: A Switchboard Operator Simulator, On Real Hardware
items.summary: After having been around computer games since the end of the 1970s, one might think that, to borrow a Who lyric, from Soho down to Brighton, you must have played them all. Games get flashier, have more depth, or longer stories, but substantially they fit into familiar categories. Then along comes [Mark Sidell] with a Western Electric telephone switchboard , and changes all that. We ain’t seen nothing like it, in any amusement hall. The premise of this game is simple. In front of you is a real 1950s telephone switchboard, and you play the operator at a hotel. Your job is to route calls between guests, hotel-functions, and external lines. There are sixty characters on the line, and 120 scenes played out over the phone. Behind the scenes is a PC with a multichannel sound card, and perhaps most importantly the switchboard hasn’t been modified. It’s a board with a history, having been used at the Southern California Edison office before being given to its former operator, and then donated to the Connections Museum. It’s thus really unusual in that it retains all of its internal hardware, something frequently removed in decommissioned boards to save weight. There’s a video below which shows it in action, and if you’re like us, we think you’d want to give it a go too. We like this project for its novelty, its attention to detail, and above all, for its respect of the original hardware. Meanwhile, it’s not the first piece of venerable telephone hardware we’ve brought you . I worked a summer at a Boy scout camp where the scouts that worked in the mission control area had to man the switchboard overnight. items.title: Ask Hackaday: Putting the C in CPU
items.summary: I was once in a meeting where the facilitator asked us to introduce ourselves with the usual information, but also wanted us to share our favorite hobby. I spent a second trying to think of which hobby I could say to not sound like a total nerd. Then I realized it didn’t matter. All my hobbies are nerdy, including designing CPUs and their instruction sets. I actually started sketching out an instruction set when I was a kid, back when no one had home computers. I am glad I lost that notebook: it would be painful to see today. The first CPU I put on an FPGA wasn’t of my own design, though. I implemented BLUE from Caxton Foster’s Computer Architecture book . I also extended it and modernized it a lot. I really wanted a C compiler for it. That’s really the problem. C was once a simple language, but modern C is far from simple, and compilers are huge projects. I have looked before at porting GCC to a different architecture, and it looks daunting. There’s LLVM, which is a bit more modern, but also non-trivial to port. There are a few older compilers that ought to be easier, but they often aren’t quite modern enough. Plus, if your CPU were big enough, which BLUE isn’t, GCC or a similar modern compiler would be attractive because you could use it to get Linux going. Keep in mind, though, I’m not talking about a C compiler that runs on BLUE. Just a cross-compiler. My OneDer CPU is 32-bit and could host a C compiler, though. That’s another reason to bite the bullet and do a “big” compiler port. Because even if BLUE isn’t that big, other CPUs are, and I’d love to have a GCC port under my belt. So… what do I do? items.title: Designing A Passively Morphing Quadcopter that can Fly Through Gaps
items.summary: Generally when a quadcopter attempts to occupy the same space as an immovable object, the quadcopter comes out as the loser. Although you can add active systems that detect and morph the quadcopter’s shape before trying to e.g. squeeze through a narrow tunnel, this adds a lot of complexity. In comparison, [Etor Arza] et al. chose to passively morph their quadcopter design upon encountering resistance. Their prototype can change its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm, which is demonstrated to fly through gaps as small as 15×20 cm and 40 cm long tubes. Although passively morphing quadcopter designs aren’t new, the challenge with such a design is to reliably transform and restore to nominal configuration only when needed. To achieve this they made two of the quadcopter’s arms flexible using elastic rolling cam (ERC) joints, with the details covered in the paper over at arXiv. They also ran many simulations to figure out the best angles under which to approach a narrow gap, following which the built-up tension in the ERC joint pushes the arm back into its nominal position. Great field to get into right now. I know people get queasy doing war engineering but… somebody is going to build it, in fact they are doing it right now. items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.
